title: US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin - BBC News
snippet:
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
Stephen Hubbard in the courtoomImage source, Reuters
Image caption,
Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024
ByMaia Davies
Published
21 October 2026, 10:22 BST
Updated 30 minutes ago
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday, according to Russian state media.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. He was accused of serving in a defence unit in Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
Some other releases of detained Americans from Russia have been obtained through prisoner swaps.
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and the US president had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

title: Installing Python modules — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
Installing Python modules¶
As a popular open source development project, Python has an active supporting community of contributors and users that also make their software available for other Python developers to use under open-source license terms.
This allows Python users to share and collaborate effectively, benefiting from the solutions others have already created to common (and sometimes even rare!) problems, as well as potentially contributing their own solutions to the common pool.
This guide covers the installation part of the process. For a guide to creating and sharing your own Python projects, refer to the Python packaging user guide.
Note
For corporate and other institutional users, be aware that many organisations have their own policies around using and contributing to open source software. Please take such policies into account when making use of the distribution and installation tools provided with Python.
Key terms¶
pip is the preferred installer program. It is included by default with the Python binary installers.
A virtual environment is a semi-isolated Python environment that allows packages to be installed for use by a particular application, rather than being installed system wide.
venv is the standard tool for creating virtual environments. It defaults to installing pip into all created virtual environments.
virtualenv is a third-party alternative (and predecessor) to venv.
The Python Package Index (PyPI) is a public repository of open source licensed packages made available for use by other Python users.
The Python Packaging Authority is the group of developers and documentation authors responsible for the maintenance and evolution of the standard packaging tools and the associated metadata and file format standards. They maintain a variety of tools, documentation, and issue trackers on GitHub.
Changed in version 3.5: The use of venv is now recommended for creating virtual environments.

Hongwu Emperor
The Hongwu Emperor (21 October 1328 – 24 June 1398), personal name Zhu Yuanzhang, was the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1368 to 1398. Born into a peasant family in Anhui, Zhu grew up amid famine, epidemics, and unrest under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. Orphaned at 16, he briefly lived as a novice monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352. Rising rapidly, he captured Nanjing in 1356, established a regional regime, and defeated rival rebels. In 1368, he proclaimed the Ming dynasty, adopted the era name Hongwu, and expelled the Yuan from China proper. During his 30-year reign, he restored stability after decades of war, strengthened state institutions, promoted agriculture, and maintained a disciplined army while seeking to limit civilian suffering. He died in 1398 and was succeeded by his grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by Zhu Di, later known as the Yongle Emperor. (Full article...)

title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide? - BBC News
snippet:
How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?
An aerial view of the Jackdaw site inside a blue Verify frame
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondendent
Published
28 minutes ago
The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Map showing the north of Scotland, the Orkney and Shetland Islands, the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. The Jackdaw gas field is marked on the map in the sea to the east of Aberdeen.
Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.
But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.

snippet:
Accessibility
Contents
BBC accessibility policy

The BBC has a long tradition of making information available and accessible. It seeks to be open and accountable and already provides the public with a great deal of information about its activities. BBC Information operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week, handling telephone and written comments and queries, and the BBC's website bbc.co.uk provides an extensive online information resource.
BBC accessibility policy
In keeping with its public service remit, and its obligations under the Disability Discrimination Act, the BBC will ensure that its media is accessible to people who have visual, hearing, motor or cognitive impairments.
Accessibility is a partnership between site producers like the BBC and the creators of the operating system, browser, and specialist assistive technologies which many disabled users employ to allow them, for example, to view websites in easier-to-read colours, with larger fonts, or as spoken text.
As such technologies have become more available and sophisticated, the BBC will:
Ensure that its media work well with these assistive technologies to ensure an accessible experience for disabled users.
Provide the 'Accessibility Help' site which will guide users in customising their computers (either by explaining the accessibility features of their operating systems or browser, or by introducing them to the range of assistive technologies which are available) to provide them with the most accessible web experience, not just for bbc.co.uk but all websites.
The BBC will also work with those in the wider accessibility community to support the future development of these technologies and the standards that allow all websites to be created to work best for them.

title: Missing German WW2 U-boat discovered off Devon 82 years on - BBC News
snippet:
Missing German WW2 U-boat found 82 years on
An underwater view of a submarine wreck, with fish swimming around it.Image source, Gasperados
Image caption,
The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944
ByJohnny Rutherford and Britta ZeltmannDevon
Published
6 hours ago
A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on.
Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).
The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently.
Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.
Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."
After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.
Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.
Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival.
"They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.

Python built-ins reference¶
Python comes with a number of built-in functions and classes.
The built-in classes include data types that would normally be considered part of the “core” of a language, such as numbers and lists. For these types, the Python language core defines the form of literals and places some constraints on their semantics, but does not fully define the semantics.
The built-ins also include functions and exceptions — objects that can be used by all Python code without the need of an import statement. Some of these are defined by the core language, but many are not essential for the core semantics and are only described here.
See also
In addition to the built-ins, Python provides an extensive importable standard library, see The Python standard library.

Billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio launches India's biggest share sale
7 hours ago
Rachita PrasadBBC News, Mumbai
LightRocket via Getty Images A security guard talks on his phone standing next to the logo of Jio on the wall.LightRocket via Getty Images
The Jio Platforms IPO is expected to be the biggest in the country
India's second richest man Mukesh Ambani's digital and telecommunications venture is tapping public investors for the first time in what's expected to be the country's largest share sale.
Jio Platforms, a unit of conglomerate Reliance Industries Ltd, aims to raise 302bn rupees ($3.2bn; £2.8bn) in the initial public offering (IPO) of freshly issued shares from Wednesday.

History of the software¶
Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands as a successor of a language called ABC. Guido remains Python’s principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.
In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us) in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the software.
In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team. In October of the same year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became Zope Corporation. title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
snippet:
Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
16 hours ago
Brandon Drenon
AFP Christina Applegate pictured wearing a black top and smiling towards the cameraAFP
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.
"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.
"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

Second Test, Gqeberha (day four of five)
South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81
Australia 3-1: Smith 28; Jansen 5-33
Australia trail by 422 runs
Australia were forced to follow-on for only the third time in the past 38 years after being dismissed for 99 by South Africa on day four of the second Test in Gqeberha.
Left-armer Marco Jansen took a superb 5-33 and Kagiso Rabada and Wiaan Mulder two wickets each as the Proteas roared back into the Test to give them a real shot at leveling the series.
They were 110-6 early on day three, their hopes severely dented, but scrapped to 425-9 after Temba Bavuma's 179 and now take a 326-run first innings lead.
Australia's surrender was stark.
After opener Nic Maddinson was dismissed late on day three, South Africa took the remaining nine wickets inside 40 overs on the fourth day.
Steve Smith was the tourists highest scoring with 28. No other batter passed 14 and the highest partnership was just 23.
The last time Australia were forced to follow-on was against India at Sydney in 2019. Before that, the most recent previous occasion was the fourth Ashes Test at Trent Bridge in 2005.
It was also the biggest first-innings deficit they conceded since a Test against West Indies in November 1984.
How Australia's collapse unfolded
Jansen sparked the collapse by nicking off nightwatchman Scott Boland with his first ball of the day at the start of the second over.
Four overs later he pinned Travis Head lbw on review for 14 and Marnus Labuschagne was brilliantly caught at slip by Simon Harmer off the bowling of Anrich Nortje for the same score.

Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.
The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.
Now a third attempt has been made to rescue the female using nets to guide her back to the open sea.
It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.

title: C API and ABI Stability — Python 3.15.0 documentation
snippet:
C API and ABI Stability¶
Unless documented otherwise, Python’s C API is covered by the Backwards Compatibility Policy, PEP 387. Most changes to it are source-compatible (typically by only adding new API). Changing existing API or removing API is only done after a deprecation period or to fix serious issues.
CPython’s Application Binary Interface (ABI) is forward- and backwards-compatible across a minor release (if these are compiled the same way; see Platform Considerations below). So, code compiled for Python 3.10.0 will work on 3.10.8 and vice versa, but will need to be compiled separately for 3.9.x and 3.11.x.
There are two tiers of C API with different stability expectations:
Unstable API, may change in minor versions without a deprecation period. It is marked by the PyUnstable prefix in names.
Limited API, is compatible across several minor releases. When Py_LIMITED_API is defined, only this subset is exposed from Python.h.
These are discussed in more detail below.
Names prefixed by an underscore, such as _Py_InternalState, are private API that can change without notice even in patch releases. If you need to use this API, consider reaching out to CPython developers to discuss adding public API for your use case.
Unstable C API¶
Any API named with the PyUnstable prefix exposes CPython implementation details, and may change in every minor release (e.g. from 3.9 to 3.10) without any deprecation warnings. However, it will not change in a bugfix release (e.g. from 3.10.0 to 3.10.1).
It is generally intended for specialized, low-level tools like debuggers.
Projects that use this API are expected to follow CPython development and spend extra effort adjusting to changes.
Stable Application Binary Interfaces¶
Python’s Stable ABI allows extensions to be compatible with multiple versions of Python, without recompilation.
Note
For simplicity, this document talks about extensions, but Stable ABI works the same way for all uses of the API – for example, embedding Python.
